title: 〜に〜をあげる・くれる・もらう (giving and receiving things)
meaning: Express giving and receiving things. Choose 「あげる」, 「くれる」, or 「もらう」 depending on who gives to whom.
connection: A は B に noun を あげる／A が (私に) noun を くれる／A は B に (から) noun を もらう

senses.label: Giving to others
senses.meaning: 「あげる」 means “I (or my side) give to someone else”, or “a third person gives to another third person”. The direction is outward from the speaker's side. It cannot be used when someone gives something to me.
senses.connection: A は B に noun を あげる (あげます／あげた)
examples: I gave my mother flowers on Mother's Day.
Tanaka gave Yamada some chocolate.
You can have this book.

senses.label: Someone gives to me
senses.meaning: 「くれる」 means “someone gives to me (or to someone on my side)”. The direction is inward, toward the speaker. When the receiver is “me”, 「私に」 is usually left out.
senses.connection: A が (私に) noun を くれる (くれます／くれた)
examples: A friend gave me a birthday present.
My older sister gave my younger sister some sweets. (told from the younger sister's side)
My dad doesn't give me any pocket money.

senses.label: Receiving from others
senses.meaning: 「もらう」 takes the receiver as the subject: “get something from someone”. The giver is marked with 「に」 or 「から」. It works both for “I received” and for “a third person received”.
senses.connection: A は B に／B から noun を もらう (もらいます／もらった)
examples: I got a dictionary from an older student.
I got a bonus from the company.
My little brother got a watch from his grandfather.

notes: When someone else gives something to me (or my family), only 「くれる」 works. Using 「あげる」 turns it into “I gave to someone else”: ✕「友達が私に本をあげた」→ ○「友達が（私に）本をくれた」.
Using plain 「あげる・くれる・もらう」 with superiors, teachers, or clients sounds rude: ✕「先生にお土産をあげました」→ ○「先生にお土産をさしあげました」. When they give to you, say 「くださる／いただく」.

Handing something over in person with 「これ、あげます」 sounds condescending, like “here, I'm letting you have this”, and is especially rude to elders and clients. When giving a gift, people usually say 「これ、どうぞ」 or 「よろしければ召し上がってください」.
The subject of 「もらう」 is the receiver, and the giver is marked with 「に／から」. To say “I gave Tanaka a book”, don't use an awkward viewpoint like ✕「田中さんは私に本をもらった」; say 「私が田中さんに本をあげた」.
Between two people outside your own circle, use 「あげる」, not 「くれる」: ✕「田中さんが山田さんに本をくれた」→ ○「田中さんが山田さんに本をあげた」.

etymology: 「あげる」 originally meant “to raise, lift up” (上げる); from “offering upward” it came to mean “give”. 「くれる」 comes from the old verb 「くる (呉る)」, which already meant “give (to someone below)”. 「もらう」 originally meant “to ask for and receive”. In modern Japanese these giving/receiving verbs are usually written in kana.
formation: Each of the three verbs carries a fixed direction. 「あげる」 was originally 「上げる」 (to raise): you “lift” something out from your side and hand it over, so the direction is “my side → outside”. 「くれる」, written 「呉る」 in classical Japanese, originally meant giving something to “this side (downward)”, so the direction is “outside → my side”. 「もらう」 originally meant “to ask for and receive”; it centers on the receiver, so the subject is the receiver and the giver is marked with 「に／から」, which show the source. The same event can be told from the giver's or the receiver's viewpoint (「友達がくれた」＝「友達にもらった」), and Japanese requires the speaker to always pick the verb while standing on “my side”. That is why these verbs can't be swapped freely.

similar.title: 〜さしあげる・いただく・くださる (honorific giving and receiving)
similar.explanation: Same origin (honorific version): the direction is exactly the same, but these are used with superiors and clients: 「あげる→さしあげる」, 「くれる→くださる」, 「もらう→いただく」. Using the plain forms of this pattern with elders sounds rude.

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern gives a “thing”, while 「〜てあげる」 gives an “action” (doing something for someone). 「本をあげた」 means you gave someone a book; 「本を読んであげた」 means you read the book to them.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「くれる」 after a te-form means someone does something for me. The direction is the same as when giving things, “outside → my side”: 「友達が手伝ってくれた」.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: Same origin: the receiver is the subject and gets an “action” from someone. 「先輩に辞書をもらった」 means you got a dictionary; 「先輩に辞書を貸してもらった」 means you received the favor of having one lent to you.

title: 〜さしあげる・いただく・くださる (honorific giving and receiving)
meaning: Honorific ways to give and receive things: 「さしあげる」 for giving to a superior, 「くださる」 when a superior gives to me, and 「いただく」 for receiving from a superior.
connection: B に noun を さしあげる／A が noun を くださる／A に (から) noun を いただく

senses.label: Giving to a superior
senses.meaning: 「さしあげる」 is the humble form of 「あげる」. My side gives something to a superior, an elder, or a guest. It raises the receiver.
senses.connection: (私は) 目上の人に noun を さしあげる (差し上げる)
examples: I presented my teacher with a bouquet.
We are giving a commemorative gift to customers who visit our store.

senses.label: A superior gives to me
senses.meaning: 「くださる」 is the respectful form of 「くれる」. A superior or elder gives something to me (or my side). It raises the giver. The masu-form is 「くださいます」.
senses.connection: 目上の人が (私に) noun を くださる (くださいます／くださった)
examples: The company president gave us some souvenirs.
My teacher gave me a dictionary.

senses.label: Receiving from a superior
senses.meaning: 「いただく」 is the humble form of 「もらう」. With my side as subject, it means receiving something from a superior. It is also the humble way to say “eat” or “drink”.
senses.connection: (私は) 目上の人に／から noun を いただく (頂く)
examples: I received a congratulatory gift from the department manager.
I received a letter from my teacher.
We received valuable feedback from our customers.

notes: The masu-form of 「くださる」 is 「くださいます」, not ✕「くださります」. The past is 「くださいました」.
Don't mix up direction and particles. When a superior gives you something, say 「社長が（私に）くださいました」 or 「社長にいただきました」. ✕「社長が私にいただきました」 would mean “the president received it”, the exact opposite.
Saying 「先生にこれをさしあげます」 to a superior's face sounds like you're bestowing a favor or pushing it on them, which is rude. When handing something over in person, 「どうぞ」 or 「よろしければお使いください」 is enough.
「いただく」 is also the humble form of 「食べる・飲む」 and can only be used for yourself: ✕「どうぞ、いただいてください」→ ○「どうぞ、召し上がってください」.
Don't use 「さしあげる」 for juniors, animals, or plants: ✕「犬にえさをさしあげる」 sounds comical. Say 「えさをあげる／やる」.

etymology: 「さしあげる」 is the prefix 「差し」 (for emphasis) + 「上げる」, meaning “to hold up with both hands and offer”. 「いただく」 originally meant “to put on top of one's head” (頂く); people once raised gifts from superiors above their heads out of respect, which led to the meaning “receive”. 「くださる」 comes from the respectful form of 「下す」, meaning “to bestow (from above)”.
formation: All three replace the plain giving and receiving verbs with words that contain “up” or “down”, showing respect through spatial relations. 「さしあげる」＝ the intensifying prefix 「差し」＋「上げる」, literally “to hold up with both hands and offer”: you lower yourself and send the thing “upward”, so it is humble language that elevates the receiver. 「いただく」 originally meant “to place on top of one's head”: you raise what you're given above your head as you accept it, so the subject is me and it is humble. 「くださる」 comes from 「下す」 (to hand down from above); the subject is the superior, so it is respectful language. Remember “when I give, it goes up; when they give to me, it comes down”, and you won't mix up the directions and subjects.

similar.title: 〜に〜をあげる・くれる・もらう (giving and receiving things)
similar.explanation: Same origin (plain version): the direction is exactly the same; this pattern is its honorific version. Use 「あげる・くれる・もらう」 with friends and family, and switch to 「さしあげる・くださる・いただく」 with superiors and clients.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「いただく」 after a te-form, so what you receive changes from a “thing” to an “action”: 「先生に本をいただいた」 (I received a book) →「先生に本を貸していただいた」 (the teacher kindly lent me a book).

similar.title: 〜てくださる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「くださる」 after a te-form means a superior does something for me: 「社長がお土産をくださった」 (gave me something) →「社長が駅まで送ってくださった」 (did something for me).

similar.title: 〜てさしあげる
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「さしあげる」 after a te-form means doing something for a superior, but it still carries a sense of bestowing a favor, so saying it to a superior's face is even riskier than giving things with this pattern.

meaning: The humble form of 「〜てもらう」. It means having a superior or someone else do something for me, with a feeling of gratitude.
connection: Verb te-form + いただく (いただきます／いただいた)

senses.label: Receiving a kindness
senses.meaning: With my side as subject, it means receiving a favor in the form of an action from a superior. It carries thanks. The person who does the action is marked with 「に」.
senses.connection: 目上の人に verb te-form + いただく／いただいた
examples: My teacher kindly corrected my essay.
The department manager kindly drove me to the station.
Thank you for taking the time to come despite your busy schedule.

senses.label: Asking someone to do
senses.meaning: Used to state a request or rule for the listener. Softer and more polite than a direct command. Common in service, announcements, and business.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただきます／いただくことになります／いただけますか
examples: Please write your name here.
I'd like you to read the materials before the meeting.
Could you wait a moment, please?

notes: The subject is “I”, and the doer is marked with 「に」: 「先生に教えていただいた」. ✕「先生が教えていただいた」 would mean “the teacher received teaching (from someone)”. Say 「先生が教えてくださった」 instead.
Use it only for actions that benefit you and deserve thanks. For trouble others cause you, use the passive: ✕「隣の人にたばこを吸っていただいた」→ ○「隣の人にたばこを吸われた」.
When talking to clients about your own company's boss, don't use respectful language toward the boss: ✕「弊社の部長に説明していただきます」→ ○「部長の田中からご説明いたします」.
「こちらに書いていただきます」 is polite but is really a one-sided instruction. When you need the other person's cooperation, 「〜ていただけますか」 or 「〜ていただけませんか」 is softer.

etymology: 「いただく」 originally meant “to put on top of one's head” (頂く). People once raised gifts from superiors above their heads out of respect, so it became the humble form of 「もらう」. After a te-form, what is received expanded from things to actions and favors.
formation: Built from te-form ＋「いただく」. The te-form presents the preceding action as “something the other person does”, and 「いただく」 is the humble form of 「もらう」, originally “to receive respectfully, raising it above one's head”. Together they mean “to humbly accept the other person's action as a favor”, so the subject is the benefiting “I”, and the doer is marked with 「に」, which shows the source. Because the structure is “receiving a favor”, the sentence naturally expresses gratitude and can only be used for actions that benefit you. When 「〜ていただきます」 is used to explain rules, it amounts to “I will receive this action from you”, which makes it a polite instruction.

similar.title: 〜てもらう
similar.explanation: Same origin (plain version): the structure, subject, and particles are identical; 「いただく」 is the humble form of 「もらう」. Say 「手伝ってもらった」 to friends and 「手伝っていただいた」 to superiors.

similar.title: 〜てくださる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: it describes the same event from the opposite viewpoint. 「先生に教えていただいた」 has me as the subject, 「先生が教えてくださった」 has the teacher; the particles 「に／が」 can't be swapped.

similar.title: 〜お〜いただく・ご〜いただく
similar.explanation: Same origin (more formal): turn the verb into 「お＋masu-stem／ご＋Sino-Japanese noun」 and add 「いただく」, as in 「お待ちいただく」 and 「ご確認いただく」. In business writing it's more common than 「〜ていただく」.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Same origin: a request made with the negative question of the potential form of 「いただく」. 「〜ていただく」 mostly describes favors already received or one-sided explanations; to ask someone, use 「〜ていただけませんか」.

meaning: The respectful form of 「〜てくれる」. A superior or someone else does something for me (or my side). It raises the doer and expresses gratitude.
connection: Verb te-form + くださる (くださいます／くださった)

senses.label: A superior does it for me
senses.meaning: With the doer as subject, it means a superior, elder, or client did something for my side. It raises the other person and carries gratitude.
senses.connection: 目上の人が verb te-form + くださる／くださいました
examples: My teacher explained it to me carefully.
The company president came all the way to the station to pick me up.
It's all thanks to everyone's support.

senses.label: Polite request
senses.meaning: The negative question 「〜てくださいませんか」 asks someone to do something. It is more polite than 「〜てください」 and close to 「〜ていただけませんか」.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くださいませんか／くださいますか
examples: Could you speak a little more slowly, please?
Would you sign this document, please?

notes: The subject is the other person (the doer), marked with 「が」: 「先生が教えてくださった」. With me as the subject, it becomes 「先生に教えていただいた」; the particles of the two patterns can't be mixed.
The masu-form is 「くださいます」 and the past is 「くださいました」, not ✕「くださります」.
When talking to clients about people in your own company, don't use 「〜てくださる」: ✕「部長が手伝ってくださいました」→ ○ (to outsiders)「部長の田中が手伝いました」.
The beneficiary must be on “my side”. Between two people unrelated to you, use plain respectful language: ✕「先生が田中さんに説明してくださった」→ ○「先生が田中さんに説明なさった」 (the former works only if Tanaka is on your side).

etymology: 「くださる」 was the respectful form of 「下す」 (くだす, “to bestow from above”), meaning “(a superior) grants”. As an auxiliary after a te-form, it means a superior grants the favor of an action, making it the respectful form of 「くれる」.
formation: Built from te-form ＋「くださる」. 「くださる」 comes from 「下す」 (to hand down from above) and is the respectful form of 「くれる」, with the giver as subject. With a te-form in front, the “thing given” becomes an “action”: a superior bestows an action on my side. Because the direction is fixed as “superior → my side”, the beneficiary must be on my side, and the pattern both elevates the other person and expresses gratitude. Turn it into the negative question 「〜てくださいませんか」 and you're asking them to grant that favor; simplify it into the imperative and you get the everyday 「〜てください」.

similar.title: 〜てくれる
similar.explanation: Same origin (plain version): the structure and direction are identical; 「くださる」 is the respectful form of 「くれる」. When a friend helps you, say 「手伝ってくれた」; when a superior helps you, say 「手伝ってくださった」.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: the same event, told in humble language with me as the subject. 「部長が見てくださった」＝「部長に見ていただいた」; the former uses 「が」, the latter 「に」.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「ください」 is simply the imperative of 「くださる」. 「〜てください」 asks or tells someone to do something; 「〜てくださる」 describes that someone did (or will do) something for me.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning (requests): 「〜てくださいませんか」 and 「〜ていただけませんか」 are about equally polite. The former asks “would you do this for me?”, the latter “may I receive this action from you?”; the latter is more common in business.

meaning: The humble form of 「〜てあげる」: my side does something for a superior or guest.
connection: Verb te-form + さしあげる (差し上げる)

senses.label: Doing for a superior
senses.meaning: The speaker's side does something for a superior, elder, or guest. It is the formal version of 「〜てあげる」. But it still implies “doing someone a favor”, so it should not be said to the person directly.
senses.connection: 目上の人に／を verb te-form + さしあげる／さしあげました
examples: I carried my teacher's bags for him.
I showed a customer the way.
I gave my seat to an elderly woman.

senses.label: Suggesting service
senses.meaning: Used when talking to a third party or when staff describe a service. When offering directly to a superior, 「お〜しましょうか」 is more appropriate.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + さしあげてください／さしあげましょう
examples: Please explain it to the customer.
Let's send the materials to the department manager.

notes: Saying ✕「先生、荷物を持ってさしあげます」 to a superior or guest sounds like “I'm doing you a favor”, which is rude. Say 「お持ちしましょうか」 or 「お持ちします」.
「〜てさしあげる」 only makes the favor sound polite; it doesn't remove the sense of bestowing it. So it's mainly used when telling a third party: 「お客様に道を教えてさしあげた」.
Using it with friends, equals, or juniors sounds overly polite or even sarcastic. With equals, 「〜てあげる」 is enough.

etymology: 「さしあげる」 is the prefix 「差し」 + 「上げる」, originally “to hold up with both hands and offer”. It became the humble form of 「あげる」. After a te-form, it means offering an action to a superior.
formation: Built from te-form ＋「さしあげる」. 「さしあげる」＝ the intensifying prefix 「差し」＋「上げる」, originally “to hold up with both hands and offer”; it is the humble form of 「あげる」. After a te-form, what's offered changes from a “thing” to “my action”, i.e. “doing something for a superior”. But its skeleton is still “I give you a favor”: the honorific only lowers the posture of giving and doesn't change the favor-giving structure. So the more directly you say it to the person who benefits, the more it sounds like you're reminding them they “owe you one”, which is why it's best not used face to face.

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: Same origin (plain version): the structure is identical; 「さしあげる」 is the humble form of 「あげる」. Use 「〜てあげる」 with equals, and 「〜てさしあげる」 when describing what you did for a superior or guest.

similar.title: お〜する・ご〜する (humble)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean “I do something for a superior”, but 「お〜する」 only lowers yourself without any sense of bestowing a favor, so it's the first choice when speaking to a superior directly: 「ご案内します」 rather than 「案内してさしあげます」.

similar.title: 〜さしあげる・いただく・くださる (honorific giving and receiving)
similar.explanation: Same origin: as a main verb, 「さしあげる」 gives a “thing” (「先生に花をさしあげた」); after a te-form, it gives an “action”.

similar.title: 〜てやる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: part of the same “doing things for others” group, but aimed the other way: 「〜てやる」 for juniors and animals, 「〜てあげる」 for equals, 「〜てさしあげる」 for superiors.

meaning: Doing something for someone below you, or for an animal or plant. It can also mean deliberately doing something to someone to “show them”, or a strong determination like “I'll show you I can”.
connection: Verb te-form + やる (やります／やった／やろう)

senses.label: Doing for someone below you
senses.meaning: Doing something for your own children, juniors, animals, or plants. More casual and blunt than 「〜てあげる」. Nowadays people often use 「〜てあげる」 for children and pets too.
senses.connection: Junior / animal / plant に／を verb te-form + やる
examples: I took the dog out for a walk.
I bought my son a bicycle.
I helped my little brother with his homework.

senses.label: Showing someone
senses.meaning: Deliberately doing something unpleasant or harmful to the other person. It has an aggressive, revenge-like tone. Common in arguments and lines in novels.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + やる／やった (often 「〜てやった」)
examples: He was so noisy that I yelled at him.
I'm going to get back at my mean older brother.

senses.label: Determination
senses.meaning: Shows the speaker's strong resolve or defiant feelings: “I'll show you”, “just watch me”. Often 「〜てやる」 or 「〜てやろう」, usually said to oneself.
senses.connection: Volitional verb te-form + やる／やろう (sentence-final)
examples: I'm definitely going to pass!
Someday I'll be the best in the world.

notes: Never use 「〜てやる」 with superiors, peers, or guests; it sounds condescending and rude. Use 「〜てあげる」 with equals and 「お〜する」 with superiors.
The “I'll show you” sense is aggressive: 「殴ってやる」 and 「言ってやる」 sound like threats or picking a fight, and saying them to someone in daily life can easily start a conflict.
In 「花に水をやる」 and 「えさをやる」, 「やる」 is the main verb “give”, not an auxiliary; in 「宿題をやる」, 「やる」 means “do”. Neither is this pattern.

etymology: 「やる」 (遣る) originally meant “to send, dispatch far away”, which extended to “give (to someone below, or to animals and plants)”. As an auxiliary after a te-form, it means doing an action for someone below you. From “inflicting something on someone” came the meanings “show them” and “I'll show you I can”.
formation: Built from te-form ＋「やる」. 「やる」 (遣る) originally meant “to send out, send far away”, and later “to give (to people of lower status, animals, or plants)”. After a te-form, what's sent out becomes an “action”, so it means doing something for juniors or animals. If the action you impose is one the other person doesn't want, it becomes “I'll show you”; aim that force of “imposing” at your own goal, and you get the resolve of “I'll definitely…”. The core is always “from above, imposed one-sidedly”, so it can't be used with superiors or peers.

similar.title: 〜てあげる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both mean doing something for someone. 「〜てあげる」 is for equals and neutral in tone; 「〜てやる」 is for juniors and animals, casual and condescending. Nowadays people often say 「〜てあげる」 to children and pets too.

similar.title: 〜てさしあげる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: part of the same “doing things for others” group. From the lowest to the highest target: 「〜てやる」→「〜てあげる」→「〜てさしあげる」.

similar.title: 〜てやる (fierce resolve)
similar.explanation: Same origin: covers the “I'll definitely…” / “I'll show you” use of 「〜てやる」 (N1 level), as in 「絶対に見返してやる」, with strong emotion and will.

meaning: Asks someone to do something for you, softly, using a negative question: “Could you ... for me?”. More polite than 「〜てください」.
connection: Verb te-form + もらえませんか／くれませんか (casual: 〜てもらえない？／〜てくれない？)

senses.label: Could I have you...?
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらえませんか」 takes “me” as the subject. Literally, “Can't I receive ... from you?”. Polite and indirect. Used with coworkers, store staff, and strangers.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + もらえませんか／もらえますか
examples: Excuse me, could you take a picture for me?
Could you hold this bag for a moment?
Could you get back to me by tomorrow?

senses.label: Would you...?
senses.meaning: 「〜てくれませんか」 takes the other person as the subject. Literally, “Won't you ... for me?”. Slightly more direct than 「もらえませんか」, but still a polite request.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれませんか／くれますか
examples: Would you close the window?
Could you explain it once more?

senses.label: Casual request
senses.meaning: With friends and family, use the plain forms 「〜てくれない？」 and 「〜てもらえない？」 for a friendly tone. Say them with rising intonation.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + くれない？／もらえない？／くれる？
examples: Hey, can you pass me the salt?
Can you give me a hand?

notes: The subject of 「もらえませんか」 is “I”, while the subject of 「くれませんか」 is the other person, so don't mix the particles: ✕「あなたに手伝ってくれませんか」→ ○「手伝ってくれませんか」／「（あなたに）手伝ってもらえませんか」.
Don't drop the potential 「もらえ」: ✕「手伝ってもらいませんか」 means “shall we get someone to help us?”. ○「手伝ってもらえませんか」.
Using 「〜てくれませんか」 with superiors or clients isn't polite enough; switch to 「〜ていただけませんか」 or 「〜てくださいませんか」.
The casual 「〜てくれない？」 and 「〜てもらえない？」 are only for friends and family; using them with coworkers or seniors sounds too casual.

etymology: Built from 「もらえる」, the potential form of the auxiliary 「〜てもらう」, or from 「〜てくれる」, plus the negative question 「〜ませんか」. Making a request as a negative question is a common way in Japanese to leave the choice to the listener and sound indirect.
formation: Built in two layers: a giving-receiving auxiliary ＋ a negative question. 「〜てもらえる」 is the potential of 「〜てもらう」, meaning “can I receive this action from you?”; 「〜てくれる」 means “you do it for me”. Add the negative question 「〜ませんか」 (“can't you…?”), and the speaker presupposes “it might not be possible”, leaving the listener room to refuse, which makes it sound gentle. 「もらえませんか」 asks from my side as the one who benefits, while 「くれませんか」 asks directly about the other person's willingness, so the former sounds a bit more indirect and polite.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, more polite: same structure, with 「もらう」 replaced by the humble 「いただく」. Use this form with superiors and clients.

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both ask someone to do something, but 「〜てください」 is a direct request or instruction that leaves no room to refuse, while 「〜てもらえませんか」 uses a question to leave the choice to the listener, so it's softer.

similar.title: 〜てほしい・〜てもらいたい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express “wanting someone to do something”. 「〜てほしい」 states your own wish and sounds pushy when said directly to the person; 「〜てもらえませんか」 asks whether they can do it, so it's a request.

meaning: A very polite request for someone to do something for you: “Could you possibly ...?”. Used with superiors, clients, and strangers.
connection: Verb te-form + いただけませんか (more formal: いただけないでしょうか)

senses.label: Could you possibly...?
senses.meaning: The negative question of the potential form of 「いただく」. With “me” as subject, it literally means “Can't I humbly receive your ...?”. One of the most common polite requests.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただけませんか／いただけますか
examples: Could you please say that once more?
Could you tell me how to read this kanji?
Could you wait a moment, please?

senses.label: Extra-formal request
senses.meaning: 「〜ていただけないでしょうか」 is softer and more formal than 「ませんか」. Use it when the request is a big one or the listener's status is very high.
senses.connection: Verb te-form + いただけないでしょうか
examples: Would it be possible to extend the deadline by a week?
Would you be willing to write me a letter of recommendation?

notes: Don't drop the potential 「いただけ」: ✕「〜ていただきませんか」 means “shall we have someone do it for us?”. ○「〜ていただけませんか」.
To ask permission to do something yourself, use the causative: ✕「休んでいただけませんか」 (would you please rest?) → ○「休ませていただけませんか」 (would you let me rest?). The subject is completely different.
When asking clients or superiors, people usually start with a cushion phrase like 「恐れ入りますが」 or 「お忙しいところ申し訳ありませんが」; otherwise it can sound stiff even with this pattern.
Using it with friends or family sounds distant or even sarcastic. Between people who are close, use 「〜てもらえない？」 or 「〜てくれない？」.

etymology: Built from 「いただける」, the potential form of 「〜ていただく」, plus the negative question 「〜ませんか」. Literally “Can't I receive your ...?”, it softens a request twice: once with humble language and once with a negative question.
formation: Built from te-form ＋「いただける」＋「ませんか」. 「いただく」 is the humble form of 「もらう」 with “I” as subject; in the potential 「いただける」, the sentence becomes “may I receive this action from you?”, asking whether it's possible on my side rather than demanding anything of the other person. The negative question 「ませんか」 then adds the presupposition “probably not, right?”. Stacking humble language, the potential, and a negative question brings the pressure of the request down to a minimum, which is why it's the standard request in business. Replace 「ませんか」 with the conjectural 「ないでしょうか」 to add one more layer of uncertainty, and it becomes even more formal.

similar.title: 〜てもらえませんか・〜てくれませんか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, slightly less polite: same structure, but 「もらう」 isn't humble. Use it with coworkers, shop staff, and strangers; with superiors and clients, use 「〜ていただけませんか」.

similar.title: 〜てくださる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜てくださいませんか」 is about as polite as this pattern. The former has the other person as the subject, the latter has me; this pattern is more common in business.

similar.title: 〜ていただく
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is the negative question of the potential form of 「〜ていただく」. 「〜ていただく」 describes favors already received; for requests, use 「〜ていただけませんか」.

similar.title: 〜ていただけるとありがたい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, even softer: instead of asking directly, you say “I'd be grateful if you could…”, presenting the request as your own feeling. Common in emails.

meaning: Expresses that the speaker wants someone else to do (or not do) something: “I want you to ...”, “I hope ...”.
connection: (person に) verb te-form + ほしい／もらいたい; negative: verb nai-form + でほしい

senses.label: Wanting others to do
senses.meaning: Expresses a wish for someone else to do something. The one who wishes is the speaker; the doer is someone else, marked with 「に」. It can also express a wish for something to happen (「早く春が来てほしい」).
senses.connection: Person に verb te-form + ほしい／ほしかった
examples: I want my mother to live a long life.
I hope the rain stops soon.
I'd like you to help me with this job.

senses.label: Wanting others not to do
senses.meaning: 「〜ないでほしい」 means you'd like the other person not to do something. It is softer than 「〜ないでください」 and conveys the speaker's feelings.
senses.connection: Verb nai-form + でほしい
examples: I'd rather you didn't smoke here.
I'd like you not to tell anyone about this.

senses.label: Wanting help
senses.meaning: 「〜てもらいたい」 is 「〜てもらう」 + 「たい」. It means basically the same as 「〜てほしい」, but sounds a little more formal. The polite version is 「〜ていただきたい」.
senses.connection: Person に verb te-form + もらいたい／いただきたい
examples: I'd like you to submit this document by the end of today.
I'd really like you to take a look at it sometime.

notes: 「〜てほしい」 and 「〜たい」 have different subjects, and mixing them up changes the meaning completely: 「先生に説明してほしい」 means you want the teacher to explain; 「先生に説明したい」 means you want to explain to the teacher.
Saying 「〜てほしいです」 or 「〜てもらいたいです」 directly to superiors or clients sounds like you're imposing a demand, which is rude. Use 「〜ていただけませんか」 or 「〜ていただけると助かります」 instead.
It only expresses the speaker's wish (the listener's in questions). For a third person, use 「〜てほしがっている」 or 「〜てほしいと言っている」: ✕「母は私に帰ってほしい」.
When the doer is a person, it's usually marked with 「に」: 「彼に来てほしい」. For things and natural phenomena, use 「が」: 「早く雨がやんでほしい」.

etymology: 「ほしい」 (欲しい) is an adjective meaning “wanted, desired”. After a te-form, what is wanted expands from a thing to someone else's action. 「〜てもらいたい」 combines the auxiliary 「もらう」 with the wish ending 「たい」.
formation: 「〜てほしい」＝ te-form (someone else's action) ＋ the adjective 「ほしい」 (want). 「ほしい」 originally only took “things” (「車がほしい」); putting a te-form in front switches what you want from a “thing” to “someone else's action”, giving “want someone to do”. 「ほしい」 is an adjective for the speaker's inner feelings, so the sentence is by default “my” wish, and for a third person you add 「がる」. 「〜てもらいたい」＝「〜てもらう」 (receive an action from someone) ＋「たい」 (I want), with the logic “I want to receive this action from you”, so the two mean basically the same thing. Because the latter contains a giving-receiving verb, it can be upgraded directly to the honorific 「〜ていただきたい」.

similar.title: 〜たい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express wishes, but 「〜たい」 is “I want to do it myself” and 「〜てほしい」 is “I want someone else to do it”. 「行きたい」 means “I want to go”; 「行ってほしい」 means “I want you to go”.

similar.title: 〜がほしい
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same adjective 「ほしい」. With “noun ＋がほしい”, you want a thing; with 「〜てほしい」, you want someone's action: 「時計がほしい」／「時計を直してほしい」.

similar.title: 〜てもらえませんか・〜てくれませんか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are about getting someone else to act. 「〜てほしい」 states your own wish, while 「〜てもらえませんか」 makes a request to the person; when asking face to face, the latter is more appropriate.

similar.title: 〜たいものだ・〜てほしいものだ
similar.explanation: Same origin, stronger tone: adding 「ものだ」 to this pattern expresses a heartfelt, emotional wish, often an expectation of society or others: 「もっと平和な世の中になってほしいものだ」.

meaning: Causative form + a giving/receiving verb. Asks for permission to do something yourself, or humbly says “allow me to ...”.
connection: Causative te-form (〜させて／〜せて) + ください／もらう／いただく

senses.label: Let me do it
senses.meaning: 「〜させてください」 directly asks the listener to let you do something. It shows an eager, proactive attitude.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + ください
examples: Please let me handle that job.
Let me think about it for a bit.
I'm not feeling well, so please let me go home early.

senses.label: Being allowed to do
senses.meaning: 「〜させてもらう」 means you did something after getting the other person's permission (or kindness). It carries thanks. 「〜させてもらえませんか」 politely asks for permission.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + もらう／もらえませんか
examples: My friend let me stay at his place for a night.
Could I use your restroom for a moment?

senses.label: Doing it humbly
senses.meaning: 「〜させていただく」 is humble language: “allow me to ...”. It is often used to formally announce your own action, as in speeches and notices.
senses.connection: Causative te-form + いただきます／いただけませんか
examples: Well then, allow me to begin my presentation.
We are closed today.
May I explain this matter briefly?

notes: Drop the causative and the meaning flips from “let me do it” to “you do it”: 「説明してください」 (please explain) ↔「説明させてください」 (please let me explain).
Don't add an extra 「さ」 to the causative of godan verbs (さ入れ言葉): ✕「行かさせていただきます」→ ○「行かせていただきます」; ✕「読まさせて」→ ○「読ませて」.

Using 「〜させていただく」 where no permission is needed at all sounds wordy and overly humble; 「本日休業させていただきます」, for example, is often criticized. When you really are asking permission, it's perfectly appropriate.
「見せてください」 means “please show me”; 「見させてください」 means “please let me look”. The doer is different, so don't confuse them.

etymology: Made from the causative 「〜させる」 (make/let someone do) + the giving/receiving auxiliaries 「くれる」 (imperative 「ください」), 「もらう」, and 「いただく」. Literally, “please give me the favor of letting me do it”, that is, “please allow me to do it”.
formation: Built from the causative 「〜させる」 (make/let someone do) ＋ the giving-receiving auxiliaries 「くれる（ください）／もらう／いただく」. The person “let” do the action in the causative is the speaker, i.e. “(you) let me do it”. The giving-receiving verb then treats this “permission” as a favor from the other person: 「させてください」＝ “please give me ‘letting me do it’”, i.e. asking permission; 「させてもらう」＝ “I received the favor of ‘being allowed to do it’”, i.e. did it with permission. Switch to the humble 「いただく」, and 「〜させていただきます」 becomes a formal announcement: “with your permission, I will do it”. In every form, the doer is always the speaker; the other person only gives permission.

similar.title: 〜(さ)せていただく
similar.explanation: Same origin (humble): 「〜させていただく」 is the humble form of this pattern's 「〜させてもらう」. It's covered separately at N3, including its formal use for announcing your own actions and the problem of overuse.

similar.title: 〜せる・〜させる (causative)
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is the te-form of the causative plus a giving-receiving verb. On its own, the causative 「させる」 means “make or let someone do”; add 「ください／もらう」, and the person being “let” becomes the speaker.

similar.title: 〜てもいい
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜てもいいですか」 also asks permission, but only asks “is it OK?”; 「〜させてください」 carries an eager “please let me do it”, so it sounds more proactive.

title: 〜させられる (causative-passive)
meaning: Combines the causative and the passive. It means being made to do something you don't want to do. It can also mean that something stirred your feelings or thoughts.
connection: Ichidan verbs, する, 来る: 〜させられる; godan verbs: 〜せられる／〜される (short form)

senses.label: Being made to do
senses.meaning: The subject is the person forced to act; the one forcing is marked with 「に」. It means “to be made to do something against one's will”, with a tone of suffering or complaint.
senses.connection: Person に causative-passive verb (食べさせられる／行かされる／させられる)
examples: As a kid, my mother made me eat vegetables I hated.
An older coworker made me drink.
I was kept waiting at the station for a whole hour.

senses.label: Can't help feeling
senses.meaning: Something makes the subject naturally feel or think something. Often used with 「考える」, 「感動する」, 「驚く」, and 「反省する」. There is no complaint about being forced.
senses.connection: 「考えさせられる」, 「感動させられる」, 「驚かされる」, etc.
examples: This movie really made me think about a lot of things.
His hard work is truly amazing.

notes: The subject is the person forced to act, the exact reverse of the causative: 「母は私に掃除をさせた」 (Mom made me clean) ↔「私は母に掃除をさせられた」 (I was made to clean by Mom). Swap the subject and 「に」, and the meaning reverses.
Only godan verbs have the short form 「〜される」, and not those ending in 「す」: ✕「話さされる」→ ○「話させられる」. Ichidan verbs can't either: ✕「食べさされる」→ ○「食べさせられる」.
The causative-passive carries a sense of reluctance, so don't use it for things you were glad to do: ✕「先生にスピーチをさせられて嬉しかった」→ ○「先生にスピーチをさせてもらって嬉しかった」.
「残業させられた」 and 「飲まされた」 sound clearly like complaints; saying them in front of your boss or clients at work makes you sound dissatisfied.

daily.example: That documentary really made you think, didn't it?

work.title: An evaluation in a report
work.description: News or commentary describing something thought-provoking.
work.example: This accident makes us think again about how important safety management is.

etymology: Formed by stacking the causative auxiliary 「せる・させる」 and the passive auxiliary 「られる」: 「させ + られる」. The godan short form 「〜される」 comes from simplifying the 「せら」 in 「〜せられる」, and it is more common in speech.
formation: Built by stacking the causative 「させる」 (A makes B do) and the passive 「られる」. First the causative sets up “someone makes me do it”, then the passive shifts the viewpoint to the one being forced, so the subject is the doer, and the one doing the forcing steps back into 「に」, which marks the source. The Japanese passive often carries a sense of “suffering”, so stacked on the causative it means “being forced to do something you don't want to”. When what “makes me” is not a person but a film or an experience, it becomes the spontaneous “can't help but…”. The godan form 「〜される」 is a colloquial contraction of 「せら」 into 「さ」 in 「〜せられる」, which is why only godan verbs can contract.

similar.title: 〜せる・〜させる (causative)
similar.explanation: Same origin: the causative takes the one doing the forcing as subject (「母が私に野菜を食べさせた」), the causative-passive takes the one being forced (「私は母に野菜を食べさせられた」). Both describe the same event.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: Same origin: this pattern is the causative plus the passive. The plain passive is “someone did something to me” (「母に叱られた」); the causative-passive is “someone made me do something” (「母に謝らせられた」).

similar.title: 〜させられる (can't help but ...)
similar.explanation: Same origin: covers the “can't help but…” sense of 「〜させられる」, as in 「深く考えさせられる」. The subject is the person moved by something, with no resentment at being forced.

similar.title: 〜させてください・〜させてもらう
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, opposite attitude: both are “someone has me do it”. 「〜させてもらう」 is doing it willingly with permission, with gratitude; 「〜させられる」 is doing it reluctantly under pressure, with dissatisfaction.

title: 〜られる・〜える (potential form)
meaning: The potential form of verbs. It means being able to do something, or that something is possible under certain conditions.
connection: Godan verbs: change the final u-row sound to the e-row + る (書く→書ける); ichidan verbs: 〜られる (食べる→食べられる); 来る→来られる; する→できる

senses.label: Ability
senses.meaning: The subject has the ability to do something. The object is usually marked with 「が」, though 「を」 is also possible. Like “can” or “know how to”.
senses.connection: Noun が godan verb e-row + る (泳げる・話せる・読める)
examples: I can speak a little Japanese.
My little brother can't swim yet.
Can you read this kanji?

senses.label: Possible under conditions
senses.meaning: Something is possible in a certain situation or under certain conditions. It has nothing to do with personal ability; it depends on outside circumstances.
senses.connection: Ichidan verb 〜られる (食べられる・来られる・見られる)／godan verb e-row + る
examples: Is this water drinkable?
Can you come to the party tomorrow?
You can take photos of Mt. Fuji from here.

senses.label: ら-dropping (ら抜き言葉)
senses.meaning: In casual speech, ichidan verbs and 「来る」 often drop the 「ら」: 「見れる」, 「食べれる」, 「来れる」. Very common in conversation, but use 「〜られる」 in formal writing and on tests.
senses.connection: Ichidan verb 〜れる (casual): 見れる・食べれる・寝れる
examples: I couldn't sleep much last night.
Can you come tomorrow?
You can watch this movie online.

notes: Don't stack the potential form with 「ことができる」: ✕「話せることができる」→ ○「話せる」 or 「話すことができる」.
「わかる」 and 「できる」 already include the meaning “can”, so they have no potential form: ✕「わかれる」 means “to separate”, something completely different.
The standard potential of 「来る」 is 「来（こ）られる」, and of 「見る」 it is 「見られる」. ら-dropped forms like 「来れる」 and 「見れる」 count as errors in exams and formal writing.
「見える・聞こえる」 can't be replaced with the potential form: ✕「眼鏡がないと字が見られない」→ ○「眼鏡がないと字が見えない」.
For ichidan verbs, 「〜られる」 looks the same as the respectful form, so asking a superior 「先生は辛い物が食べられますか」 can sound like you're questioning their ability. When asking them, 「召し上がりますか」 is better.

etymology: The ichidan 「られる」 comes from the classical auxiliary 「らる」, which once covered four meanings: spontaneous, potential, passive, and honorific. Godan potential forms (書ける, etc.) developed after the Edo period by simplifying forms like 「書かれる」, and became independent “potential verbs”. 「ら抜き」 is ichidan verbs changing by analogy with the godan potential verbs.
formation: Ichidan verbs: stem ＋「られる」. 「られる」 comes from the classical auxiliary 「らる」, whose basic meaning is “something comes about naturally”; from “under these conditions it can happen” came “be able to”, which is why it shares its form with the passive, respectful, and spontaneous uses. The godan potential (書ける) is generally thought to have split off as an independent “potential verb” when forms like 「書かれる」 were simplified to “e-row ＋る”, so it conjugates like an ichidan verb (書けない, 書けます). The potential describes a state (“can or can't”) rather than an action, so the object often changes from 「を」 to 「が」: 「日本語が話せる」. ら-dropping (見れる) arose by analogy, with ichidan verbs imitating the “e-row ＋る” shape of godan potential verbs.

similar.title: 〜ことができる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both express ability or possibility. The potential form is concise and common in speech; 「〜ことができる」 is more written and formal, and simpler to form (dictionary form ＋ことができる).

similar.title: 〜が見える・〜が聞こえる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「見られる・聞ける」 means being able to see or hear given certain conditions or opportunities; 「見える・聞こえる」 means things naturally come into view or reach your ears, regardless of intent.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (respectful)
similar.explanation: Same origin: for ichidan verbs, 「〜られる」 is also the respectful form; both come from classical 「らる」. 「先生が来られる」 can mean “the teacher is coming (respectful)” or “the teacher can come”; context decides.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (passive)
similar.explanation: Same origin: for ichidan verbs, the potential and the passive are both 「〜られる」, so 「食べられる」 can mean “can eat” or “be eaten”; godan verbs have different forms (書ける／書かれる).

meaning: A sight or sound naturally reaches your eyes or ears, with no effort on your part: “can be seen”, “can be heard”.
connection: Noun + が + 見える／聞こえる

senses.label: Can be seen
senses.meaning: 「見える」 means something naturally comes into view. The object takes 「が」. It's an intransitive verb, outside the person's control.
senses.connection: Noun が 見える (見えます／見えない)
examples: You can see Mt. Fuji from the window.
It's so dark I can't see anything.
Without my glasses, I can't see well.

senses.label: Can be heard
senses.meaning: 「聞こえる」 means a sound naturally reaches your ears. The object takes 「が」. It is also outside your control.
senses.connection: Noun が 聞こえる (聞こえます／聞こえない)
examples: I can hear music from the next room.
Sorry, I can't hear you very well.
I heard birds singing in the distance.

notes: 「見える」 and 「聞こえる」 are intransitive verbs, so the object takes 「が」: ✕「富士山を見える」→ ○「富士山が見える」.
They can't express deliberately looking or listening: ✕「毎晩テレビが見える」→ ○「毎晩テレビを見る」; ✕「音楽が聞こえるのが好きだ」→ ○「音楽を聞くのが好きだ」.
「お見えになる」 and 「〜様がお見えです」 are respectful forms of 「来る」 (a guest has arrived), not “can see”. They're common when receiving guests.
「〜に見える」 and 「〜く見える」 mean “look like…”: 「若く見える」 (look young) and 「若い人が見える」 (I can see a young person) mean completely different things.

etymology: 「見える」 comes from 「見る」 plus the classical spontaneous auxiliary 「ゆ」 (見ゆ→見える), meaning “to come into view naturally”. 「聞こえる」 likewise comes from 「聞く」 + 「ゆ」 (聞こゆ→聞こえる). So both naturally carry the idea of “happening on its own, not by will”.
formation: 「見える」 comes from 「見る」＋ the classical spontaneous auxiliary 「ゆ」 (見ゆ→見える), and 「聞こえる」 from 「聞く」＋「ゆ」 (聞こゆ→聞こえる). 「ゆ」 means “happens on its own”, so these words don't mean “I go and look or listen” but “a sight or sound enters my eyes or ears by itself”. The main player is the thing seen or heard, so they are intransitive: the object becomes the subject with 「が」, and the person seeing takes 「に」 (「私には見えない」). From “naturally coming into view” came “look like” (「〜に見える」) and “(a guest) appears” (「お見えになる」).

similar.title: 〜られる・〜える (potential form)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「見られる」 and 「聞ける」 mean being able to see or hear given certain conditions or opportunities (「この映画館で古い映画が見られる」); 「見える」 and 「聞こえる」 mean things naturally come into view or reach your ears.

similar.title: 〜が見られる
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「〜が見られる」 is mostly written and means “(a phenomenon or trend) can be observed”, as in 「若者の読書離れが見られる」; 「見える」 focuses on a scene naturally entering your field of vision.

similar.title: 〜く見える・〜に見える
similar.explanation: Same origin: the same verb 「見える」; after adjectives and nouns it means “look like…”: 「彼は年より若く見える」.

similar.title: 〜とみえる
similar.explanation: Same origin: derived from 「見える」, it expresses an inference based on what you see, “it seems…”: 「誰も来ないところをみると、中止になったとみえる」.

meaning: A respectful pattern that describes the actions of the listener or a superior more respectfully, raising the doer.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + になる; ご + kanji action noun + になる

senses.label: Native Japanese verbs
senses.meaning: Shows respect for the actions of superiors and guests. The subject is the other person. More respectful than 「〜れる・〜られる」.
senses.connection: お + verb masu-stem + になる (お読みになる・お帰りになる・お待ちになる)
examples: The president has already gone home.
Have you read this book, professor?
Please, go ahead and use this seat.

senses.label: Kanji nouns
senses.meaning: Put 「ご」 before a kanji action noun. Common examples are 「ご覧になる」 (see), 「ご利用になる」 (use), and 「ご出席になる」 (attend).
senses.connection: ご + kanji noun + になる (ご覧になる・ご利用になる)
examples: Did you see yesterday's news?
This card can be used at our stores nationwide.

notes: Use it only for the actions of the listener or superiors, never for yourself: ✕「私がお書きになります」→ ○「私がお書きします」 (humble).
If a verb has a special respectful form, use that: ✕「お見になる」→ ○「ご覧になる」; ✕「お行きになる」→ ○「いらっしゃる」; ✕「お言いになる」→ ○「おっしゃる」.
Don't stack 「られる」 on top: ✕「お帰りになられる」 is a double honorific. In formal settings, 「お帰りになる」 is enough.
When talking to clients about your own company's boss, don't use respectful language: ✕「部長はお出かけになりました」→ ○「部長の田中は外出しております」.

etymology: 「お」 is a respectful prefix (from 「御 (おほみ)」), and 「になる」 originally means “to become”. Literally, “(your action) naturally becomes ...”. Instead of saying the other person “does” something directly, it uses this indirect “becoming” to show respect.
formation: Built from the respectful prefix 「お／ご」＋ the masu-stem (used as a noun) ＋「になる」. Here the masu-stem works as a noun (「帰り」, 「書き」), and adding 「お」 makes it an honorific term for the other person's action. 「になる」 basically means “to become”, so the whole phrase literally says “(your) going home comes about”. Japanese honorifics often avoid saying directly that the other person “does” something, presenting their action as “happening naturally” so as not to pass judgment on a superior, which is why 「お〜になる」 sounds respectful. It's generally thought that because the verb must first become a noun, verbs with one-syllable stems like 「見」 and 「寝」, which don't easily form nouns, use special expressions such as 「ご覧になる」 and 「お休みになる」 instead.

similar.title: 〜れる・〜られる (respectful)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: both are respectful language, but 「書かれる」 is slightly less respectful than 「お書きになる」 and easily confused with the passive and potential. When speaking directly to clients and superiors, 「お〜になる」 is safer.

similar.title: いらっしゃる・おっしゃる (special respectful verbs)
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: verbs with special respectful forms (行く・来る・言う・見る, etc.) don't use 「お〜になる」; use 「いらっしゃる」, 「おっしゃる」, 「ご覧になる」, and so on.

similar.title: 〜お〜です (honorific)
similar.explanation: Same origin: also a respectful expression built on 「お＋masu-stem」; with 「です」 it's more concise and usually describes the other person's state or current action: 「社長がお待ちです」.

similar.title: お〜ください
similar.explanation: Same origin: also turns the other person's action into a respectful noun with 「お＋masu-stem」. 「お〜になる」 describes their action; 「お〜ください」 asks them to do it.

meaning: The respectful version of 「〜てください」, politely asking someone to do something. Common in customer service, announcements, and notices.
connection: お + verb masu-stem + ください; ご + kanji action noun + ください

senses.label: Native Japanese verbs
senses.meaning: Uses respectful language to request or instruct. More polite than 「〜てください」. Common from store staff, in station announcements, and in business.
senses.connection: お + verb masu-stem + ください (お待ちください・お入りください)
examples: Please wait a moment.
Please, come in.
Please feel free to contact us.

senses.label: Kanji nouns
senses.meaning: Put 「ご」 before a kanji action noun. Common for reminders and requests in notices, emails, and announcements.
senses.connection: ご + kanji noun + ください (ご注意ください・ご確認ください)
examples: Please watch your step.
For details, please see our website.
Please check the contents.

notes: Don't mix in the humble 「する」: ✕「お待ちしてください」→ ○「お待ちください」; ✕「ご注意してください」→ ○「ご注意ください」. Even native speakers often make this honorific mistake.
If a verb has a special respectful form, use it: ✕「お見ください」→ ○「ご覧ください」; ✕「お来ください」→ ○「お越しください」; ✕「お食べください」→ ○「召し上がってください」.
It's still an imperative. When asking a superior or client to do something for you, 「お〜いただけますか」 or 「〜ていただけませんか」 is softer; 「お〜ください」 suits invitations that benefit the other person, or notices.
「お水ください」 is 「〜をください」 (please give me a thing) with 「を」 dropped, not this pattern. In this pattern, 「お」 is followed by a verb's masu-stem.

etymology: Made from the respectful prefix 「お／ご」 + the verb's masu-stem (used as a noun) + 「ください」, the imperative of 「くださる」. Literally, “please grant me your ...”. Turning the action into a noun avoids a direct command and shows respect.
formation: Built from 「お／ご」＋ the masu-stem (used as a noun) ＋「ください」. 「ください」 is the imperative of 「くださる」 (a superior bestows), literally “please grant (us) …”. The 「お＋masu-stem」 in front turns the other person's action into a respectful noun, so the whole means “please grant (your) waiting”: rather than ordering them directly, you ask them to “give” an action. Compared with 「〜てください」 (te-form ＋ください), it adds a step of wrapping the action in a respectful noun, so it's more respectful. And precisely because 「ください」 is itself respectful, you can't insert the humble 「する」 in the middle (✕お待ちしてください).

similar.title: 〜てください
similar.explanation: Same origin, less respectful: also ends in 「ください」 to ask someone to do something. 「待ってください」→ the more polite 「お待ちください」; shop staff, announcements, and notices usually use the latter.

similar.title: お〜になる
similar.explanation: Same origin: also uses 「お＋masu-stem」 to turn the other person's action into a respectful noun. 「お〜になる」 describes their action; 「お〜ください」 asks them to do it.

similar.title: 〜ていただけませんか
similar.explanation: Similar meaning, softer: a request in question form that leaves the choice to the listener. When asking someone to do something for you, 「ご確認いただけませんか」 is more polite than 「ご確認ください」.

similar.title: お〜願う・お〜願います
similar.explanation: Similar meaning: 「お待ち願います」 and 「ご協力願います」 are also requests used in notices and announcements, but more formal and written in tone.
